# Make the test suite trustworthy {#sec-test-suite}

- The tests greta relies on to know it still works: what they cover,
  how long they take, and whether a passing run means anything.
  Grouping label: `testing`.
- Nothing here is user-facing, which is exactly why it needs its own
  milestone rather than being distributed into releases.

**Why this milestone exists again.** An earlier draft of this plan
dissolved the testing and documentation milestones and scattered their
issues into whichever release touched the same files. The reasoning was
that ongoing work cannot carry a version, and every milestone had to
carry one. That rule has been dropped: milestones are now work buckets
and releases are cut when a batch is ready, so a milestone no longer
implies a version. With the constraint gone, the argument for scattering
goes with it - and scattering had a real cost, because it made the
testing work invisible as a body of work and left each release
carrying a test refactor that had nothing to do with its theme.

**What the work is.** Three strands.

*Coverage and correctness of the harness itself*:
[#433](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/433) (get as close to
100% coverage as is sensible),
[#727](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/727) and
[#751](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/751) (tests for
`check_for_free_state_error()` and `as_tf_function()`, both currently
untested),
[#596](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/596) (edge cases for
`gradient_descent()`), and
[#723](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/723) (break up the
`check_*` functions in `test_posteriors.R`, which are what the
posterior checks actually assert through).

*Modernising testthat usage*:
[#563](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/563) and
[#591](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/591) (`expect_no_error()`
and friends over the home-grown `expect_ok`),
[#715](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/715) (custom
expectations written the formal way),
[#695](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/695) (snapshot tests
for `calculate()`), and
[#395](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/395) (`patrick` for
the parameterised cases).

*Making the suite runnable*:
[#624](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/624) (speed),
[#708](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/708) (replace
`skip_if_not(check_tf_version())` with something that does not silently
skip everything when Python is missing), and
[#408](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/408) (dockerfiles for
development and for users).

**Start with [#708](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/708).** A test suite that skips silently when the Python
stack is unavailable reports success while testing nothing, which makes
every other issue in this milestone harder to reason about. The Geweke
gate is the precedent: `test_posteriors_geweke.R` disabled itself
outright until August 2026, and nobody noticed because the run was
green.

## Sprint item: the conformance suite {#sec-conformance}

*Not a GitHub issue, and not yet agreed.* This originated in the design
book's initial draft (commit `96c09a1`, July 2026) rather than in any issue or
maintainer decision, and it has been carried through every restructure since
without sign-off. Treat it as a proposal. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Drafted issue body, unfiled

Written but not filed, pending the decision above.

*Proposed title: Build a conformance suite: pinned log-densities, gradients, and bijector round-trips*

greta has no fast, deterministic way to answer the question "did this change
alter the numbers greta produces?". That question comes up on every TensorFlow
version bump, and it will come up constantly during the op-dictionary and
node-registry rework, where the whole point is to change how the numbers are
computed while keeping them identical.

#### What exists today

Seven `test_posteriors_*.R` files: `binomial`, `bivariate_normal`,
`chi_squared`, `lkj`, `standard_uniform`, `wishart`, and `geweke`. Six run on
every PR through `R-CMD-check`; the Geweke checks are gated behind
`GRETA_GEWEKE=true` and run weekly, because they cost roughly 33 minutes for
three samplers.

These are end-to-end statistical checks. They catch gross breakage, but they
are slow, stochastic, and they tell you a sampler is wrong rather than which
log-density or gradient moved.

#### What is missing

A layer underneath them that is fast, deterministic, and specific:

1. **Pinned log-densities.** For each distribution family, evaluate the
   log-density at fixed parameter values and fixed data, computed once against
   a known-good greta and stored as package data. greta has 29 distribution
   constructors in `R/probability_distributions.R`.
2. **Pinned gradients.** The same fixtures, comparing the gradient of the
   log-density with respect to the free state. Samplers depend on the gradient,
   not just the value, and a gradient can break while the density stays right.
3. **Bijector round-trips.** For every constrained variable type, check that
   the forward and inverse transforms compose to the identity, and that the
   log-Jacobian adjustment is what it should be. The constructors are in
   `variable_node$create_tf_bijector()` at `R/node_types.R:303`, dispatching to
   the `tf_scalar_*_bijector()` family for the none/low/high/both/mixed
   constraint cases.

#### Why it belongs in the test-suite milestone

It was originally scheduled alongside the TensorFlow unpin, on the reasoning
that the unpin was the first change that would need it. The unpin shipped
without it, so it is unbuilt and its first real consumer is now the backend
work. Putting it here rather than there means that milestone does not have to
build its own oracle before it can start.

#### Acceptance

- A fixture file of pinned values, generated by a documented script so it can
  be regenerated deliberately rather than by accident.
- Tests that compare against the fixtures within a stated tolerance, and that
  fail loudly with the offending distribution named.
- The suite runs in seconds, on every PR, without the Python stack having to
  produce a posterior.

#### Open questions for whoever picks this up

- What tolerance? Too tight and a harmless TFP change breaks CI; too loose and
  it stops catching anything.
- Do the fixtures get regenerated on a deliberate numerical change (e.g. TFP
  0.25 changing how `lkj_correlation()` and `wishart()` sample), and if so, what
  is the review process for accepting a new fixture?
- Is 29 distributions the right granularity, or should this cover a
  representative subset plus every bijector?
:::


The plan's one genuinely new piece of test infrastructure: golden
log-density and gradient values, bijector round-trips, and Geweke tests
run against greta's *public* API. It is the acceptance oracle for any
change to what computes greta's numbers - a TensorFlow version bump, the
op dictionary and node registry in milestone 11, or a second backend.

It was originally scheduled with the TensorFlow unpin, on the reasoning
that the unpin was the first change that needed it. The unpin shipped
without it, so the suite is unbuilt and its first real
consumer is now the backend work. It belongs here rather than there
because milestone 11 should not have to build its own oracle before it
can start, and because everything else in this milestone is about
making a green test run mean something - which is the same problem.

**Approach.** Pin log-density and gradient values for a small set of
models covering each distribution family, at fixed parameter values,
computed once against a known-good greta and stored as data. Add
bijector round-trip tests for every constrained variable type. Keep the
Geweke checks as the end-to-end layer above both - they are already
written, and as of August 2026 they are finally runnable ([#722](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/722)).
